title: Evals store, the three lenses, surveys and model checks

story: Nova's harness, our program that runs Claude inside the VM, has a routing table: a list that picks the model and the effort for each kind of job. It says that a typical build runs on Opus 5.5 at medium effort. Effort is how much thinking and writing the model puts into each answer, and at medium a typical build costs about $1.63 per task. Someone asks the money question: would low effort do? Low costs about a third less. So you run the 15 quick tasks of TICKET-BENCH, our set of past fcp tickets with hidden tests, once at low effort: 11 of 15 pass. Medium passed 13 of 15 last week. Low loses 14 points, so the answer seems clear.

Out of curiosity you run medium again, with nothing changed: 10 of 15. You run it once more: 12. The same setting, on the same tasks, scored 87%, 67% and 80%. So which of those numbers is "medium", and was low's 73% really worse?
hook.question: How do we decide whether a cheaper setting is really worse, when the same setting scores differently every time it runs?

read.h: Run it three times and measure the wobble
p: A model does not do the same thing twice. Even with the same prompt, the same code and the same tests, a long agent run takes a different path each time: it reads the files in another order, tries a different fix first, and sometimes fails a task it solved yesterday. On a small suite one task matters a lot. With 15 tasks, a single task that flips from pass to fail moves the score by almost 7 points. So one run of a suite gives you the setting's real score plus some luck, and nothing in that one number tells you how much of it was luck.

That is why every case in our evals runs three times. Each pass through the whole suite is called a round, and each round has its own pass rate. The pass rate we report is the average of the three rounds, and the spread is the best round minus the worst. For medium that is 87% minus 67%, so 20 points: that is how far this setting moves on these 15 tasks when nothing changes at all. A difference smaller than the spread may be nothing but that movement.

Every suite saves its results through one small Python function, record(). It checks the rules before anything is written, computes the pass rate per round, and stores the summary next to every single run, so anyone can recompute the numbers later.

code.text:
# ai-agents/evals/results.py  (every suite calls record(); Python, like Harbor and the suites around it)
"""One JSON file per eval run. Quality, cost, steps, agents and time are scored together."""
import json
import statistics

import boto3

BUCKET = "rhino-ai-agents-eval-results"
CAUSES = {"too_many_tools", "bad_handoff", "contradicting_prompt", "missing_context", "flaky_environment"}


def record(suite: str, version: str, setup: dict, cases: list[dict], started_at: str) -> str:
    assert all(len(case["runs"]) == 3 for case in cases), "every case runs 3 times"
    runs = [run for case in cases for run in case["runs"]]
    assert all(run["cause"] in CAUSES for run in runs if not run["pass"]), "label every failure"
    per_round = [statistics.mean(case["runs"][i]["pass"] for case in cases) for i in range(3)]
    summary = {
        "pass_rate": statistics.mean(per_round),
        "pass_rate_spread": max(per_round) - min(per_round),  # small suites swing a lot; always show it
        "cost_per_case_usd": sum(run["cost_usd"] for run in runs) / len(runs),
        "median_turns": statistics.median(run["turns"] for run in runs),
    }
    key = f"{suite}/{version}/{setup['split']}/{started_at}.json"
    body = {"suite": suite, "version": version, "setup": setup, "summary": summary, "cases": cases}
    boto3.client("s3").put_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=key, Body=json.dumps(body).encode())
    return key  # the nightly job turns new keys into ai_agents_eval_<summary field> series

notes.text: The fixed list of failure causes. The weekly run review counts them, so every failed run must carry one.
A case that ran once or twice cannot show its spread, so the file is refused before it is written.
A failed run without a known cause is refused too.
The pass rate of round 1, round 2 and round 3 across all cases. Python counts True as 1 and False as 0, so the mean of passes is a rate.
Best round minus worst round. The scoreboard always draws it next to the pass rate.
Quality is never judged alone: cost per case and the median number of turns are scored in the same file.
The key says what the run was: suite, version, split and start time.
No key in the code: on a sandbox VM the credentials come from the machine's own role.

read.h: One file per run, in one store
p: Five suites produce numbers like these: TICKET-BENCH for Nova, BYTE-GOLD for Byte, our review agent, and three more for the routines, the skills and the brain. If each suite kept its own format, every comparison would mean lining up spreadsheets by hand. So all of them call the same record() and write one JSON file per run into one S3 bucket. That bucket is the eval store.

The key of each file reads like a sentence, for example ticket-bench/0.4.1/smoke/2026-11-03T02-20-00Z.json: the suite, the harness version under test, the split and the start time. A split is a named slice of a suite. smoke is a quick slice of 15 tasks, dev is the slice people work against every day, and holdout is kept for the final check, so that nobody tunes a prompt until it fits those cases by accident. Every night the metrics job reads the new files and turns each summary into series for the eval scoreboard, which draws every pass rate together with its low edge, the pass rate minus the spread.

deeper.h: Go deeper: who writes and who reads the store
p: The suites run on sandbox VMs, the same short-lived machines Nova works on, and a VM never holds a key. It writes to the bucket with the machine's own role, the permission AWS attaches to the instance, and the request stays inside AWS through the S3 VPC endpoint. The nightly metrics job runs in GitHub Actions and reads new files with a separate read-only role, which it gets through GitHub's OIDC login, so the reader can never change a result.

JSON files plus Grafana is a deliberately small choice. Products made for agent traces, such as Langfuse, bring their own database to run. What five suites from five teams need first is one format, and a bucket of files with a fixed key gives exactly that.

read.h: The rule for moving a setting
p: Now the decision. A sweep is a small eval run that tries settings next to each other. For each job in the routing table it runs the setting the table has today, one level of effort below and one level above, three rounds each on the same split. Then one rule decides: keep the cheaper setting if its pass rate is at least the current pass rate minus the current spread. Put simply, if the cheaper setting lands inside the wobble of today's setting, the suite cannot tell the two apart, so we take the cheaper one.

Back to the story. Over three rounds medium scores 78% with a spread of 20 points, so its low edge is 58%. Low scores 69%. That is lower, but it is inside medium's wobble, so the rule keeps low and saves about a third on every typical build. The rule works the same way upwards: high costs $2.41 a task, so it must beat medium by more than the spread, 98%, to earn its price. It scores 91%, which looks like a big win and is not one, so nothing moves up.

The rule does not prove that low is as good as medium. It says that this suite cannot see a difference. That is why the nightly evals keep running after the switch: if low really is worse, the gap shows up over the following weeks, and the row moves back up. And no agent changes the routing table. The change is one pull request to the harness that links the scoreboard, and a person approves it.

code.text:
# ai-agents/evals/sweeps/2026-w9-effort.yaml
# Confirms the routing table on our code before real pilot tickets. Results go to the eval store.
vm_size: wide
repeats: 3                          # report the spread, never a single run
suites:
  ticket-bench: { split: smoke }    # 15 tasks
  byte-gold:    { split: dev }      # never the holdout
rows:                               # the table's current setting first, then one level each side
  - job: build_typical
    suite: ticket-bench
    settings: [opus-5-5/medium, opus-5-5/low, opus-5-5/high]
  - job: build_hard
    suite: ticket-bench
    settings: [opus-5-5/high, opus-5-5/medium, opus-5-5/xhigh]
  - job: review_logic_security
    suite: byte-gold
    settings: [opus-5-5/medium, opus-5-5/low, opus-5-5/high]
  - job: review_conventions
    suite: byte-gold
    settings: [sonnet-5-5/low, sonnet-5-5/medium, opus-5-5/low]
effort_changes: per message         # keeps the prompt cache warm
decision:
  keep_cheaper_if: its pass_rate >= current pass_rate - current spread
  if_a_row_loses_quality: move that row one level up
  apply_as: one harness PR that links the scoreboard; a person approves it

notes.text: Wide VMs are the largest sandbox size; a sweep runs many cases at once.
Three rounds, so every setting has a spread.
The holdout slice stays untouched, so it can still catch a setting tuned to the cases people see.
The current setting comes first; the rule compares the other two with it.
Per message, not per session: the Go deeper panel below explains why that keeps the prompt cache.
The low edge: the current pass rate minus the current spread.
A person approves the change; the sweep only proposes it.

deeper.h: Go deeper: changing effort without losing the cache
p: The routing table can change effort inside one session, for example a plan at high and a small follow-up at low. How you change it matters for cost. Claude's prompt cache reuses the start of a conversation as long as that start stays exactly the same. On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, the API can change effort per message (a beta feature), and the earlier messages stay unchanged, so the cache still matches. Changing the request's top-level effort instead changes the prompt from the start, and the cache begins again. That is what the line effort_changes: per message means.

Anthropic's own guidance for Opus 5.5 says to run an effort sweep on your own evals instead of carrying settings over from an earlier model. Most numbers in our routing table started as Anthropic's suggestions, and the sweep is how they become ours.

read.h: The same rule for a new model
p: The harness is more than the model. Around each run sit parts we added because the model needed help: the plan grill, which asks the requester questions before planning; a self-review subagent; the QA agent; the scope judge, which vetoes changes the ticket did not ask for; nudges from the progress watcher; and the kb skill, which searches the brain pages. Every part costs tokens and time on every run. When a newer model ships, some parts stop helping, because the model now does that job by itself. Anthropic has removed a whole step from its own harness for exactly this reason.

So every new model gets the same check, with the same rule. First, run each suite with every part on: that is the reference. Then switch off one part at a time, with all the others still on, and run three rounds again. A part goes only if the pass rate stays above the reference's low edge without it, and the cost or the time falls. Switching off two parts at once would hide which one mattered. We also run the check once on today's model, so that on the day a new model ships there is already a baseline to compare with.

code.text:
# ai-agents/evals/sweeps/new-model.yaml
# Run when a new model ships, and once in W12 on today's model as the reference.
model_under_test: claude-opus-5-5         # replace with the new model's ID
reference: { model: claude-opus-5-5, harness: current }
repeats: 3
suites: [ticket-bench/smoke, byte-gold/dev, routine-bench/weekly, skill-evals/nightly, brain-qa/nightly]
harness_parts:                            # each one is switched off alone; all others stay on
  - self_review_subagent
  - qa_agent
  - scope_judge
  - progress_watcher_nudges
  - plan_grill
  - kb_skill
runs:
  - { name: full, model: "{model_under_test}", parts_off: [] }
  - { name: without-each-part, model: "{model_under_test}", parts_off: each }
decision:
  move_model_if: every suite's pass_rate >= reference pass_rate - spread, and cost per case doesn't rise
  drop_part_if: pass_rate stays within the spread without it, and cost or time falls
  apply_as: the monthly rule-diet PR; a person approves it

notes.text: The reference is today's model with today's harness.
Each part has a flag in the harness that switches it off.
each expands into one run per part, with only that part off.
The same low-edge test as the effort sweep, plus a saving.
Removals go into a monthly pull request that a person approves.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the team-level view, with the same caution
p: Evals answer one question: is a setting good on a fixed set of tasks? Whether the team actually works better is a different question, and two more tools answer it, both at team level and never per person. The first is a set of three lenses from DX, a research group that studies developer productivity: utilization (how many people use AI each week, how many PRs had AI help, how many tasks went to agents), impact (merged PRs next to change failure, and the hours of human work the agents' merged PRs stand for) and cost (AI spend in total and per engineer). Any one lens alone misleads: usage can rise while impact falls, so the three sit side by side on the delivery dashboard.

The second is a ten-question survey in October and the same ten questions in December: time saved, time lost to builds, reviews and setup, and confidence when changing code. A study by METR found developers who felt faster while they were slower, which is why the survey asks about time lost too and is read next to the metrics, never instead of them. Teams with fewer than five answers are folded into Other, and each answer is reported as a median with its IQR, the range from the 25th to the 75th percentile. It is the same habit as the spread: a number never travels without how much it moves.

lab.title: Is the cheaper setting really worse?
lab.goal: Record three settings into a local eval store, three rounds each, and let the sweep's rule decide whether the cheaper setting stays.

guess.q: Medium effort passed 13, 10 and 12 of 15 tasks in its three rounds. Low effort passed 11, 11 and 9. What does the sweep's rule do with the typical build?

options.text: It stays on medium, because low scores 9 points lower on average.
options.why: 9 points is less than medium's own spread of 20 points. Medium moves that much with nothing changed, so the suite cannot tell the two apart.

options.text: It moves to low, because low's 69% is above medium's low edge of 58%.
options.why: That is the rule: a cheaper setting inside the current setting's wobble is kept, and every typical build costs a third less.

options.text: Nothing can be decided until each setting has run 100 rounds.
options.why: More rounds would shrink the spread and give a sharper answer, but the rule is built to decide with three, and the nightly evals keep checking afterwards.

CAUSES = {"too_many_tools", "bad_handoff", "contradicting_prompt", "missing_context", "flaky_environment"}

follow.say: Write a stand-in for the quick slice of TICKET-BENCH: 15 tasks, three rounds each, with one setting. Each setting solves tasks at its own rate and costs its own price, and a fixed random seed gives you the same numbers as this page.
follow.do:
cat > fake_suite.py <<'EOF'
"""Stands in for TICKET-BENCH's smoke split: 15 tasks, each run 3 times with one setting."""
import random
import sys
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from results import CAUSES, record

SKILL = {"low": 0.70, "medium": 0.74, "high": 0.80, "xhigh": 0.82}  # how often a setting solves a task
PRICE = {"low": 1.10, "medium": 1.60, "high": 2.40, "xhigh": 3.30}  # dollars per task, roughly
PARTS = {"plan_grill": (0.0, 0.20), "kb_skill": (0.15, 0.05)}  # what switching a part off loses: skill, dollars
setting = sys.argv[1]  # for example opus-5-5/medium
parts_off = sys.argv[2:]  # harness parts to switch off, for example plan_grill
model, effort = setting.split("/")
skill = SKILL[effort] - sum(PARTS[p][0] for p in parts_off)
price = PRICE[effort] - sum(PARTS[p][1] for p in parts_off)

cases = []
for task in range(1, 16):
    runs = []
    for round_ in range(3):
        rng = random.Random("|".join([setting, *parts_off, str(task), str(round_)]))
        passed = rng.random() < skill + (task % 5 - 2) * 0.08  # some tasks are harder than others
        runs.append({
            "pass": passed,
            "cost_usd": round(price * rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2), 2),
            "turns": int(20 + 30 * skill * rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3)),
            "seconds": rng.randint(300, 900),
            "cause": None if passed else rng.choice(sorted(CAUSES)),
            "agents": rng.randint(1, 3),
        })
    cases.append({"id": f"T-{task:03}", "runs": runs})

time.sleep(1)  # a real suite takes an hour; this keeps two runs from sharing one second
started_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H-%M-%SZ")
setup = {"split": "smoke", "model": f"claude-{model}", "effort": effort, "harness": "0.4.1", "parts_off": parts_off}
print(record("ticket-bench", "0.4.1", setup, cases, started_at))
EOF

follow.say: Write the sweep's rule as a small script and let it decide. A cheaper setting stays if it reaches the current low edge; a more expensive one must clear the current high edge, the pass rate plus the spread.
follow.do:
cat > decide.py <<'EOF'
"""The sweep's rule: a cheaper setting stays if its pass rate is at least the current pass rate minus the spread."""
import json
import pathlib
import sys

current = sys.argv[1]  # the routing table's setting today, for example opus-5-5/medium
results = {}
for path in sorted(pathlib.Path("store/ticket-bench/0.4.1/smoke").glob("*.json")):
    run = json.loads(path.read_text())
    if run["setup"]["parts_off"]:
        continue  # runs with a harness part switched off belong to the new-model check
    setting = run["setup"]["model"].removeprefix("claude-") + "/" + run["setup"]["effort"]
    results[setting] = run["summary"]  # the newest run of each setting wins

now = results[current]
low_edge = now["pass_rate"] - now["pass_rate_spread"]
high_edge = now["pass_rate"] + now["pass_rate_spread"]
print(f"{'setting':16} {'pass':>5} {'spread':>6} {'$/task':>6}")
for setting, s in results.items():
    if setting == current:
        verdict = f"current: low edge {low_edge:.2f}, high edge {high_edge:.2f}"
    elif s["cost_per_case_usd"] < now["cost_per_case_usd"]:
        verdict = f"keep the cheaper one ({s['pass_rate']:.2f} >= {low_edge:.2f})" if s["pass_rate"] >= low_edge else f"too weak ({s['pass_rate']:.2f} < {low_edge:.2f})"
    else:
        verdict = f"worth the price ({s['pass_rate']:.2f} > {high_edge:.2f})" if s["pass_rate"] > high_edge else f"not worth the price ({s['pass_rate']:.2f} <= {high_edge:.2f})"
    print(f"{setting:16} {s['pass_rate']:5.2f} {s['pass_rate_spread']:6.2f} {s['cost_per_case_usd']:6.2f}  {verdict}")
EOF

solution.text:
"""The new-model check: a harness part goes only if the pass rate holds without it and the cost falls."""
import json
import pathlib
import sys

setting = sys.argv[1]
runs = [json.loads(p.read_text()) for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("store/ticket-bench/0.4.1/smoke").glob("*.json"))]
mine = [r for r in runs if r["setup"]["model"].removeprefix("claude-") + "/" + r["setup"]["effort"] == setting]
ref = [r["summary"] for r in mine if not r["setup"]["parts_off"]][-1]  # every part on
low_edge = ref["pass_rate"] - ref["pass_rate_spread"]
for r in mine:
    if not r["setup"]["parts_off"]:
        continue
    s, part = r["summary"], "+".join(r["setup"]["parts_off"])
    holds = s["pass_rate"] >= low_edge
    cheaper = s["cost_per_case_usd"] < ref["cost_per_case_usd"]
    print(f"{part:12} pass {s['pass_rate']:.2f} (low edge {low_edge:.2f})  ${s['cost_per_case_usd']:.2f} vs ${ref['cost_per_case_usd']:.2f}  {'drop it' if holds and cheaper else 'keep it'}")
# python3 parts.py opus-5-5/medium
# plan_grill   pass 0.78 (low edge 0.58)  $1.39 vs $1.63  drop it
# kb_skill     pass 0.51 (low edge 0.58)  $1.59 vs $1.63  keep it

check.q: A new prompt moves BYTE-GOLD's pass rate from 78% to 82%. The current prompt's spread is 6 points. What do you conclude?

options.text: The new prompt is better by 4 points, so ship it.
options.why: 4 points is less than the 6 points the current prompt moves with nothing changed. The suite cannot see this difference.

options.text: The suite cannot tell the two apart; the 4 points fit inside the current prompt's wobble.
options.why: A difference smaller than the spread may be luck. To count as better, the new prompt must clear 78% plus 6, so 84%.

options.text: The new prompt is worse, because its number is less certain.
options.why: Nothing says it is worse. The honest answer is that the suite cannot see a difference either way.

check.q: Why does record() refuse a file in which a case ran only once?

options.text: A single round has no spread, so nobody could tell how much of its score was luck.
options.why: The spread needs at least two rounds, and we fixed it at three. Without it, every comparison on the scoreboard would be a guess.

options.text: S3 refuses objects that are too small.
options.why: S3 stores files of any size. The rule is about what the numbers mean, not about storage.

options.text: The nightly job can only read files with exactly 45 runs.
options.why: The job reads any summary. The check sits in record() so that a file without a spread never reaches the scoreboard at all.

check.q: In the new-model check, the run without the kb skill scores 51%. The reference scores 78% with a spread of 20 points, and the kb skill costs only $0.04 per task. What happens to the kb skill?

options.text: It goes, because every part costs tokens on every run.
options.why: Saving money is only half of the rule. The pass rate must also stay above the low edge.

options.text: It goes, because $0.04 is a saving and the rule only asks for cost or time to fall.
options.why: Cost or time falling is the second condition. The first, holding the pass rate, failed.

options.text: It stays, because 51% is below the reference's low edge of 58%.
options.why: Without the part the score drops further than the wobble can explain, so the part is still doing real work.

p: The eval store is the bucket rhino-ai-agents-eval-results in the ai-agents AWS account: one Terragrunt unit in the infrastructure repo at terraform/accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/evals/results-bucket/terragrunt.hcl, from terraform-aws-modules/s3-bucket 5.13.0 with KMS encryption, versioning and no public access, applied by a person. ai-agents/evals/results.py stays Python because Harbor and the suites around it are Python. The nightly metrics job gets metrics/src/eval-results.ts with @aws-sdk/client-s3 and pushes ai_agents_eval_pass_rate, _pass_rate_spread, _cost_per_case_usd and _median_turns with suite, version, split, model and effort labels, which the eval scoreboard from the dashboards lesson draws.

The effort sweep (ai-agents/evals/sweeps/2026-w9-effort.yaml) runs in week 9 on TICKET-BENCH smoke and BYTE-GOLD dev, before real pilot tickets; its result is one harness PR to the routing table. The new-model check (new-model.yaml) runs once in week 12 on today's model as the reference, and its removals go into the monthly rule-diet PR. The three lenses are metrics/src/lenses.ts, written as delivery_lens_* series per team and week into a "Three lenses" row of delivery-impact.json; human-equivalent hours and the wording of the cost-per-hour number are Nir's decision. Shai sends the October survey from metrics/survey/questions.yaml by 21 October and the same form by 10 December, and compares them with npx tsx metrics/src/survey-compare.ts october.csv december.csv.

tickets.why: The eval store: the bucket, record() with three runs per case and a cause for every failure, and the nightly series.
The effort sweep and its rule: keep the cheaper setting while it holds within the spread.
The new-model check: each harness part switched off alone, judged by the same rule.
DX's three lenses side by side, team level only.
The October developer survey, the baseline for time and confidence.
The December survey and the comparison with medians and their ranges.

words.plain: One pass through a whole suite. Every case runs in each of three rounds.
The best round's pass rate minus the worst round's: how much a setting moves with nothing changed.
The pass rate minus the spread. A cheaper setting above it is kept.
The S3 bucket with one JSON file per eval run, written by every suite through record().
A named slice of a suite: smoke for a quick run, dev for daily work, holdout for the final check.
A small eval run that tries a setting and its neighbours side by side, three rounds each.

review.q: Medium scored 80% with a spread of 10 points; low scored 72%. Without looking, say what the sweep's rule does and why.
review.a: The low edge is 80 minus 10, so 70%. Low's 72% is above it, so the cheaper setting is kept; the 8-point gap fits inside medium's own wobble.

review.q: Name the two things record() refuses, and what would go wrong on the scoreboard without each check.
review.a: A case with fewer than three runs (no spread, so no way to judge a change) and a failed run without a cause from the list (the weekly review could not count it).

review.q: A teammate wants to switch off the plan grill and the self-review subagent in one run to save time. What do you answer?
review.a: Switch off one part at a time with the others on. Two at once hides which one mattered, and a part goes only if the pass rate holds within the spread and cost or time falls.

remember: Run every case three times and judge a change against the spread: a cheaper setting that lands inside the wobble stays, and a more expensive one must clear it.
